title: When girls rattle an autocrat’s rule
text:
When girls rattle an autocrat’s rule
Muslim girls banned from wearing headscarves to school in Azerbaijan are protesting, while some live out their religious obligation in affirmative ways that challenge the regime.
In recent weeks, ever since an autocratic government in Azerbaijan told girls they must not wear headscarves to school to ensure official secularism, protests have erupted across the mainly Muslim country.
Some girls who want to wear a hijab wept outside their schools after being barred entry. Others gathered to chant slogans and cite a constitutional right to religious freedom.
Some students, including boys, called for a boycott of public education. Some Azerbaijani women who do not wear a hijab began to put one on, out of solidarity. Many simply asked authorities to explain exactly how a headscarf disrupts learning in a classroom.
Meanwhile, in neighboring Iran and Turkey, a few leaders criticized the ban as either un-Islamic or as an attempt by Azerbaijan to gain influence in the region. (At least a fifth of Iranians are ethnic Azeris – more than twice Azerbaijan’s own population.) In recent decades, regimes in some Muslim countries – such as Iran and Turkey – have fallen over fierce struggles about women covering their heads in public.
Yet in recent days, many Azerbaijani girls have also begun to figure out that either resisting a forced code against religious dress or complying with it might only play into the regime’s ability to suppress dissent and stay in power.
They found a way to affirm the truth of their faith that would not betray their dignity and identity.
Many girls began to wear wigs to school, fulfilling a religious desire for modesty by still covering their heads and necks.
Such a simple act fits an approach defined by the famed anti-communist dissident Václav Havel of the former Czechoslovakia as “living in truth.” Wearing a wig shatters the regime’s facade of total control. It gives concrete evidence of individual freedom over the lie that Azerbaijanis have no say over their civil liberties. A charade is exposed.
As Mr. Havel often stated, “Truth and love must prevail over lies and hate.”
Secularism in government runs deep in Azerbaijan, even though more than 90% of its people are Muslim. Women there had the right to vote before those in the United States or Britain. The country established the first schools for girls in the Muslim world.
But for decades, a family dynasty has reigned. Its grip might not be ended simply by street protests. As many other countries have discovered in being liberated from a harsh ruler, a mental shift by individuals to act out their freedom and integrity – such as girls simply wearing a wig – can sometimes erode a regime, perhaps faster than mobs or coups.
